what_its_for: This medicine is used to treat certain types of cancer, including breast cancer, stomach cancer, and lung cancer that have a protein called HER2 on the cancer cells. It works by attaching to HER2-positive cancer cells and delivering a powerful chemotherapy directly into them to kill them.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion through a vein by a nurse or doctor in a clinic or infusion center. You will NOT give this medicine to yourself at home. Each infusion takes about 30 to 90 minutes. You may be given other medicines before your infusion to help prevent allergic reactions and nausea.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your body weight and the type of cancer being treated. Most patients receive an infusion once every 3 weeks (every 21 days). Do not change your dose or schedule without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss or need to reschedule your infusion appointment, call your doctor or cancer care team right away. It is very important to stay on schedule. Your team will help you find the next best time to receive your treatment.
storage: This medicine is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals at the clinic or pharmacy. You do not need to store it at home. The prepared infusion should be used right away or kept refrigerated and used within a specific timeframe handled by your care team.
what_to_avoid: Avoid becoming pregnant or fathering a child while on this medicine, as it can cause serious harm or death to an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 7 months after your last dose if you are a woman, or 4 months if you are a man. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 7 months after the last dose. Avoid people who are sick with infections, as this medicine can lower your ability to fight infections. Avoid activities that could increase your risk of bleeding or injury if your blood counts are low.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: shortness of breath, coughing, fever, or difficulty breathing (these could be signs of a serious lung problem called interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis); chest pain or irregular heartbeat; severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea; signs of infection such as fever over 100.4°F (38°C), chills, or unusual fatigue; unusual bleeding or bruising; numbness, tingling, or pain in your hands or feet; yellowing of the skin or eyes; or any signs of a severe allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing.
when_it_works: This medicine starts working right away at the cellular level, but it may take several weeks or months before you and your doctor can see how well the treatment is working. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular scans and tests. Every person responds differently, so be patient and keep all your follow-up appointments.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: This medicine must NOT be used during pregnancy or breastfeeding due to serious risks to the baby. Women who can become pregnant must use effective birth control. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects such as fatigue and nausea; your doctor will monitor you closely. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have any kidney or liver issues, as your dose may need to be adjusted. Children: The safety and effectiveness in children have not been established.
